extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students of aesthetics / fine art theory
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for creating and evaluating tragic (and generally 'touching' or 'sublime') art: what kinds of pleasure art should aim for, how moral propriety and conflict generate aesthetic effect, and how to balance intellectual and emotional appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of the fine arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The fine arts have the same aim as nature (or the Author of nature), namely, to spread pleasure and render people happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art 'procures for us in play what at other more austere sources of good to man we extract only with difficulty'—it supplies enjoyment without appreciable effort or sacrifice. This pleasurable aim is legitimate and beneficial; attempting to replace it as the chief aim with a moral aim can strip art of its freedom and charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free pleasure (distinct from sensual pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A free pleasure is that which brings into play the spiritual forces—reason and imagination—and awakens a sentiment by the representation of an idea, as opposed to sensuous/physical pleasure which depends on immediate sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free pleasure 'rests wholly upon moral conditions' and exercises moral faculties. The arts should aim at free pleasure (good, true, perfect, beautiful, touching, sublime) rather than merely sensual gratifications. Sensual pleasure is excluded from the domain of the fine arts unless ordered and represented by art (i.e., regulated into taste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral means vs moral aim in art
rubrics_metrics.description: If free pleasure rests upon moral conditions, art aiming at pleasure must proceed by moral means; but if art's chief aim is expressly moral, it loses its freedom and its aesthetic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should employ moral means to reach the pleasurable/aesthetic effect; making the moral aim primary turns recreation into serious occupation and reduces art's influence. For highest moral influence, art must exercise its liberty and aesthetic action (i.e., charm) rather than become didactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of art as necessary for influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Art's freedom—the liberty to aestheticize rather than moralize—is what gives it influence and power to complete moral work via pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A salutary moral effect from art is achieved when art is at its most free; curtailing artistic freedom in favor of an explicit moral mission diminishes its capacity to charm and thereby to move audiences morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of aesthetic sources of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: All representations that show conformity between end and means (propriety) are sources of free pleasure; they can be classified as: the good, the true, the perfect, the beautiful, the touching, the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different kinds of pleasure engage different faculties: the good especially occupies reason; the true and perfect, intelligence; the beautiful, intelligence and imagination; the touching and sublime, reason and imagination. This taxonomy can guide what aspect an artwork principally pursues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety (conformity with the aim) as the general source of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The general source of all pleasure, even sensual pleasure, is propriety—the conformity of means to ends; free pleasure arises when we represent this conformity and experience agreeable sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should aim to represent or suggest propriety (relation of means to ends) so that spectators recognize harmony; even physical pleasures are ultimately pleasurable insofar as they reflect some perceived propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of purely sensual pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensual pleasure is excluded from the domain of the fine arts unless the sensual impressions are ordered, reinforced, or moderated by an artistic plan recognized by representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sensual elements are present, only the tasteful regulation (which pleases the understanding) merits the name of art. Unregulated sensual charm belongs to life, not art.

rubrics_metrics.name: The sublime as mixed displeasure-and-pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime produces pleasure partly through a feeling of our feebleness or impotence to embrace an object, and partly through a feeling of our moral power which fears no limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sublime object thwarts physical power (causing displeasure) but recalls our higher faculty (reason), yielding joy through moral superiority. Use of grandeur that overwhelms senses but elevates reason will produce the sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The touching as tempered suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The touching is a mixed sensation of suffering and the pleasure we find in suffering; it is felt when personal misfortune is represented but tempered enough that a compassionate spectator can take pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To achieve 'touching' effect, depict personal misfortune with restraint so grief leaves room for compassionate pleasure. Example: loss that moves us long after (remembrance), and contrast between feeble and heroic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy evokes moral pleasure by subordinating physical to moral propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy pleases through mixed feelings—pleasure produced by pain—especially when physical propriety is sacrificed to moral propriety, or when one moral propriety yields to a higher one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic plots should center on conflicts where moral duty triumphs over natural/self-interested ends (or where moral dilemmas force sacrifice), because the victory of moral law amid suffering yields high moral pleasure (e.g., martyrdom, Coriolanus' sacrifice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining whether emotion yields pleasure or displeasure
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide if an emotion is pleasurable or painful we must compare the fulfilled ends to the ignored ends and see which affects us more profoundly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral significance and magnitude of ends (particularly moral propriety) determine the balance. Moral propriety typically outweighs physical ends, producing pleasure even when suffering is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering of the virtuous vs the perverse
rubrics_metrics.description: The suffering of the virtuous moves us more painfully than that of the perverse, because the former contradicts both human destiny (happiness) and the specific principle that virtue renders happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals should exploit this asymmetry: virtue's misfortune hits on multiple levels and thus elicits stronger tragic emotion; conversely, the prosperity of the wicked offends more intensely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral reparation (punishment/repentance) as aesthetic object
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment and especially repentance of wrongdoers can produce aesthetic pleasure because they reassert the moral law and display conscience triumphing over self-love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragic depiction of remorse or self-punishment (heroic despair, repentance) can be among the highest pictures of morality in action—these scenes elevate respect for the moral law and are powerful devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest moral pleasure arises from conflict/struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law awakens most vividly when it struggles against other forces (passions, instincts, physical necessity); resistance reveals the strength of moral force and yields moral pleasure accompanied by pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic emphasis on moral conflict—clearly staged internal or external opposition—enhances the depth of moral feeling and the aesthetic reward for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic poet should employ mixed feelings to secure moral pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry that secures a high degree of moral pleasure must employ mixed feelings and please through pain or distress; tragedy specializes in this approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct characters and situations where moral and natural proprieties conflict so audiences experience the dialectic of pain and pleasure that defines tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in intellectual perversity (craft) vs moral disgust
rubrics_metrics.description: We may take pleasure in the sequence and cunning of a perverse person's machinations (intellectual propriety), but this pleasure turns to indignation if moral agency is salient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists can exploit audience abstraction: directing attention to the craft of a villain's plan can create suspense and admiration of skill, but full moral appreciation requires that vice be ultimately humiliated or morally judged to preserve overall propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety-in-vice must be humbled by morality for perfect pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual propriety in vice can never be a source of perfect pleasure except when it is humiliated by morality, because moral sense must be brought into relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a villain's cleverness is to be gratifying to audiences, the narrative must later reveal or re-establish moral superiority (e.g., Clarissa's rational propriety surpassing Lovelace), thereby enhancing total pleasure through moral contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience segmentation: heart vs intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Different audiences respond differently: the crowd is affected through the heart (emotional impression) without knowing the cause, while certain connoisseurs seek the intellectual appropriateness of means to ends and may be unaffected emotionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should be aware of these classes and balance appeals: avoid relying solely on over-refined intellectual effects that fail to move the heart, and beware of alienating either group. National/cultural tendencies (e.g., French taste) may skew toward intellectualism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual appeal: harmonize moral (heart) and natural (mind) propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: When a tragic poet aims to awaken moral propriety and knowingly chooses means to that end, he can charm both connoisseurs (by intellectual propriety) and the crowd (by moral emotion)—the first satisfies the heart, the second the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately craft works that provide both visible moral integrity (for emotional response) and appropriate means/construction (for intellectual appreciation) so the piece succeeds across audience types.
